items.followUp: State four differences between a compound and a mixture.

rubric.why: A compound has a fixed composition.
rubric.description: States that elements are present in a fixed proportion.
rubric.how: Award for stating fixed composition or a definite proportion of elements.

rubric.why: Formation of a compound produces a substance with properties different from those of its elements.
rubric.description: Compares the properties of a compound with those of its constituent elements.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the compound’s properties differ from those of its constituent elements.

rubric.why: Constituent elements can be separated only through chemical change.
rubric.description: Explains how a compound can be decomposed into its elements.
rubric.how: Award for stating that chemical methods are required to separate its elements.

rubric.why: A compound has a uniform composition throughout.
rubric.description: Identifies a compound as homogeneous.
rubric.how: Award for describing the compound as homogeneous or uniform throughout.

rubric.why: Compounds have characteristic physical constants.
rubric.description: Gives a characteristic property such as a definite melting or boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning at least one definite melting or boiling point.

modelAnswer: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion by mass.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements.
Its elements can be separated only by chemical methods, not by physical methods.
A compound is homogeneous and has a uniform composition throughout.
A pure compound has definite physical constants, such as a definite melting point and boiling point.

items.followUp: Define a compound and give two examples of compounds.

rubric.why: A covalent bond forms through the sharing of electrons.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent bond as a bond formed by sharing electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the shared electron pair(s) as the basis of the bond.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Explains a single covalent bond with an example.
rubric.how: Award for the one-pair explanation and a suitable example such as H₂.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond involves two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: Explains a double covalent bond with an example.
rubric.how: Award for the two-pair explanation and a suitable example such as O₂.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond involves three shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: Explains a triple covalent bond with an example.
rubric.how: Award for the three-pair explanation and a suitable example such as N₂.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is a chemical bond formed between atoms by sharing one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond is formed by sharing one pair of electrons; for example, H₂.
A double covalent bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons; for example, O₂.
A triple covalent bond is formed by sharing three pairs of electrons; for example, N₂.

items.followUp: Explain the main observations of Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: The model places positive charge in a very small, dense central nucleus.
rubric.description: Describes the small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for identifying a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus.

rubric.why: The model explains why most alpha particles passed straight through the foil.
rubric.description: States that most of the atom is empty space.
rubric.how: Award for explicitly mentioning that the atom is mostly empty space.

rubric.why: Electrons are the negative particles in the model.
rubric.description: Identifies electrons as negative particles around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning electrons and their negative charge.

rubric.why: In Rutherford’s model, electrons move around the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for describing electrons as revolving or orbiting around the nucleus.

rubric.why: A labelled diagram should show the central nucleus, electrons, and space within the atom.
rubric.description: Provides a simple, correctly labelled representation of the model.
rubric.how: Award for a diagram or clear textual schematic showing a central positive nucleus and electrons around it, with the mostly empty space indicated.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s atomic model has the following features:
An atom has a very small, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre.
Almost all the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular paths; the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and electrons holds them in the atom.
Most of the volume of an atom is empty space.
Diagram:
e⁻
e⁻ (  [ + nucleus ]  ) e⁻
e⁻
The nucleus is at the centre, electrons are around it, and the space between them is mostly empty.

items.followUp: What is the Tyndall effect? Give one example of a colloid that shows it.

rubric.why: A colloid is heterogeneous, even though it may appear uniform to the eye.
rubric.description: States that a colloid is heterogeneous.
rubric.how: Award for identifying its actual nature as heterogeneous.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.
rubric.description: Describes the stability of colloidal particles on standing.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the particles do not settle or remain dispersed.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light.
rubric.description: Mentions light scattering or the Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award for stating that colloids scatter light or show the Tyndall effect.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles undergo continuous random motion.
rubric.description: Describes the movement of colloidal particles.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning Brownian motion or continuous random movement.

modelAnswer: A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture, although it may appear homogeneous to the naked eye.
Its particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.
Colloidal particles scatter light, producing the Tyndall effect.
The particles show continuous, random Brownian movement.

items.followUp: Write the molecular formula of carbon dioxide and explain what it tells you.

rubric.why: A molecular formula conveys the kinds and numbers of atoms in a molecule.
rubric.description: Defines molecular formula in terms of the atoms in a molecule.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it shows the kinds and numbers of atoms present in a molecule.

rubric.why: H₂O is a valid example and indicates two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example and interprets it.
rubric.how: Award for H₂O or another correct molecular formula, with a correct indication of its atoms.

modelAnswer: A molecular formula shows the kinds and actual numbers of atoms of each element present in one molecule of a substance.
For example, H₂O shows that one water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of calcium (atomic number 20) in shells.

rubric.why: Magnesium has 12 electrons arranged as 2, 8, and 2 in its shells.
rubric.description: Gives magnesium’s shell electronic configuration.
rubric.how: Award for the correct configuration 2, 8, 2.

rubric.why: The configuration shows two electrons in the outermost shell.
rubric.description: Identifies the number of outer-shell electrons.
rubric.how: Award for stating that magnesium has two valence electrons.

modelAnswer: Magnesium has atomic number 12, so a neutral magnesium atom has 12 electrons.
Its electronic configuration in shells is 2, 8, 2.
Magnesium has two electrons in its outermost shell.

items.followUp: The distance between the nuclei of two bonded hydrogen atoms is 74 pm. Calculate the atomic radius of hydrogen.

rubric.why: Atomic radius is defined as half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms.
rubric.description: Defines atomic radius using the internuclear distance of identical bonded atoms.
rubric.how: Award for stating the half-distance definition.

rubric.why: Half of the 74 pm H–H internuclear distance is 37 pm.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of atomic radius.
rubric.how: Award for the correct hydrogen example, including the value 37 pm.

modelAnswer: Atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together.
For example, the internuclear distance in an H₂ molecule is 74 pm.
Atomic radius of hydrogen = 74 pm ÷ 2 = 37 pm.

items.followUp: What determines an element’s position in the modern periodic table, and why?

rubric.why: Atomic number gives the number of protons and identifies the element.
rubric.description: States that atomic number determines an element’s identity.
rubric.how: Award for linking atomic number to the number of protons or to the identity of the element.

rubric.why: Atomic number determines electron arrangement and chemical properties, whereas isotopes of an element can have different masses.
rubric.description: Explains why atomic number is more fundamental than atomic mass.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that atomic number governs electron arrangement/properties or that isotopes share an atomic number but differ in mass.

modelAnswer: The atomic number is more fundamental than atomic mass because it gives the number of protons in an atom and therefore determines the identity of the element.
It also determines the electronic configuration and hence the chemical properties of the element.
Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different atomic masses.
